industry_realities.implication: Domestic STEM students should apply for GRFP as senior undergraduates to preserve a second attempt in year one of PhD if needed

industry_realities.common_belief: A student can apply to multiple Tri-Council agencies if their research is interdisciplinary
industry_realities.actual_reality: Applicants must submit to a single agency based on their primary research discipline; multiple submissions are not permitted
industry_realities.implication: Interdisciplinary students must make a deliberate, binding determination of primary discipline before submitting and cannot hedge across agencies

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD funding at top Canadian universities is fixed and non-negotiable
industry_realities.actual_reality: Total PhD compensation is composed of multiple stackable components: institutional base package ($18,000–$30,000/year), OGS (+$15,000/year if won), CGRS-D (to $40,000–$45,000/year with top-up), Vanier (to $50,000–$55,000/year with top-up), and supervisor top-up (variable). The range for the same student at the same institution can span from $22,000 to $55,000/year depending on awards and supervisor.
industry_realities.implication: Students should ask specific questions about base packages, award percentages, and supervisor top-up policies during admission to understand realistic total compensation

industry_realities.common_belief: The SMART Scholarship is a straightforward fellowship with no post-award obligations
industry_realities.actual_reality: SMART Scholarship requires a DoD employment commitment after graduation and summer internship participation; recipients cannot freely pursue academic or private-sector careers until the service obligation is fulfilled
industry_realities.implication: Applicants must assess post-graduation career plans before accepting SMART Scholarship; the service commitment is a binding condition

industry_realities.common_belief: Tri-Council doctoral awards represent the standard funding level for Canadian PhD students
industry_realities.actual_reality: Per Professor Bruce Arndtsen (McGill), many departments had to top up these fellowships from research grants simply to reach their normal stipend level, suggesting Tri-Council award values have historically been below institutional norms in some fields
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should not treat the CGRS-D CAD $40,000/year value as automatically sufficient or above-market for their discipline and institution

industry_realities.common_belief: The OGS application is handled federally or centrally
industry_realities.actual_reality: OGS applications are submitted through the institution's graduate studies office. Each institution sets its own internal deadline and selection criteria within provincial requirements. Results are released February–April. There is no single centralized OGS application portal.
industry_realities.implication: Students must track their specific institution's internal OGS deadline (typically October–November), not a provincial deadline, to avoid missing the application window

industry_realities.common_belief: If you get into a top-ranked PhD program, you will almost certainly finish with a degree
industry_realities.actual_reality: Even under the most favorable conditions, no more than 75% of PhD students ever complete; at many programs the 10-year completion rate is 57-63%; attrition is structural and field-wide, not a marker of individual failure
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should investigate completion rates as a standard part of program evaluation and treat programs that cannot or will not disclose this data with skepticism

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD student mental health struggles are primarily caused by individual resilience or adjustment issues
industry_realities.actual_reality: 39% of PhD students score in moderate-to-severe depression range compared to 6% of the general population — a 6x higher rate that is structural, not individual. The PhD environment itself is the primary causal factor.
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should evaluate program structures and advisor behaviors as mental health risk factors, not assume their own resilience will be sufficient to offset structural problems

industry_realities.common_belief: Most PhD graduates go into academic careers — that's the primary outcome the PhD prepares you for
industry_realities.actual_reality: In 2023, industry/business (47%) surpassed academia (34%) as the primary destination for new S&E PhD graduates; this is now the structural norm, not an exception or a fallback
industry_realities.implication: Students and programs that frame industry as the backup path are operating in an inverted reality; the majority outcome is now industry, and academic placement is the minority, above-average outcome

industry_realities.common_belief: A famous researcher with many publications will be a good PhD advisor
industry_realities.actual_reality: Mentorship is a learned skill, not a personality trait and not correlated with research output; negative mentorship behaviors (absence, credit-taking, exploitation, volatility) are completely invisible in a publication record and only detectable by talking to current and former students
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate advisors through direct investigation of their mentorship behavior, not through their research reputation; these are independent variables

industry_realities.common_belief: Bullying by supervisors in PhD programs is rare or limited to a few bad actors
industry_realities.actual_reality: 21% of PhD students report being bullied, and of those, 48% identify their supervisor as the perpetrator — meaning roughly 1 in 10 PhD students is bullied by their own advisor
industry_realities.implication: Advisor vetting should include explicit investigation of supervisory behavior, not just research output — and programs should be evaluated on whether they have structural mechanisms to address supervisor misconduct

industry_realities.common_belief: The academic job market is tough but PhD graduates who work hard enough will find faculty positions eventually
industry_realities.actual_reality: Academic placements have declined 20 percentage points across all S&E fields over 20 years (54% in 2003 to 34% in 2023), with some fields like math/statistics dropping 43 percentage points; this is a structural, multi-decade contraction, not a temporary cycle
industry_realities.implication: The academic job market is not going to recover to historical norms; students must plan for a structurally smaller academic job market, not treat current conditions as a temporary trough

industry_realities.common_belief: The funding period stated in a PhD offer letter is roughly how long the degree will take
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most PhD funding packages guarantee 4-5 years; median time to degree nationally is 7.3 years overall and 8.4-9.5 years in humanities/social sciences; the funding cliff at year 4-5 coincides with peak attrition
industry_realities.implication: Students should treat year 4-5 funding as the beginning of a vulnerable phase, not the end of the program, and ask explicitly about institutional support structures beyond the guaranteed period

industry_realities.common_belief: High student satisfaction rates in a PhD program indicate a healthy, well-functioning environment
industry_realities.actual_reality: 75% satisfaction coexists with 36% seeking mental health help, 21% experiencing bullying, and 79% reporting career uncertainty — satisfaction reflects sunk-cost commitment and meaning-making, not absence of structural problems
industry_realities.implication: Do not use program satisfaction scores as a primary quality signal; instead probe specific structural variables: advisor access, bullying incidence, mental health outcomes, and career placement data

industry_realities.common_belief: A postdoc in biology is an optional step you take if you want to do more research before industry
industry_realities.actual_reality: 57.8% of biology/biomedical PhDs go directly to postdocs — it is a mandatory structural step before competitive candidacy for permanent faculty positions, not an optional research extension
industry_realities.implication: Biology PhD career timelines must include 3-5 mandatory postdoc years; the real time-to-independent-career is 10-12 years from bachelor's, not the 5-6 years implied by PhD completion alone

industry_realities.common_belief: If a PhD student doesn't finish, it's because they weren't capable enough or didn't fit the field
industry_realities.actual_reality: CGS data shows that completion is most strongly predicted by financial support continuity, mentoring quality, social environment, and program structure — not individual ability; attrition is a structural outcome, not a personal one
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should evaluate structural factors (completion rates, funding continuity, mentorship infrastructure) rather than assuming their ability will overcome structural deficiencies

industry_realities.common_belief: Campus mental health services provide adequate support for PhD students who are struggling
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 26% of PhD students who used institutional mental health support found it helpful — meaning 74% of users did not benefit from the resources their institution provided
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should identify mental health support options outside their institution before enrolling, including private therapists covered by student insurance, and should not assume institutional availability equals functional support

industry_realities.common_belief: Program prestige and advisor reputation are the best proxies for your career outcomes as a PhD graduate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Field-level structural forces — postdoc mandates, academic placement rates, definite commitment rates at graduation — create baseline outcome probabilities that prestige modifies but does not override; most biology labs produce 10+ PhDs per tenure-track slot regardless of advisor fame
industry_realities.implication: Students must evaluate field-level career structure and program-specific placement rates, not just prestige rankings; a prestigious program in a field with 27% academic placement (math/stats 2023) still produces mostly non-academic graduates

industry_realities.common_belief: If you have a problem with your advisor, you should address it directly with them
industry_realities.actual_reality: Direct confrontation with an advisor in a power-asymmetric relationship creates retaliation risk; the National Academies recommends neutral third-party resources (ombudspersons, student advocates) as the appropriate first contact
industry_realities.implication: Students should identify and verify the existence of neutral institutional recourse mechanisms before they need them, not during a crisis; the absence of such mechanisms should be a program selection factor

industry_realities.common_belief: More than half of PhD students who want academic careers will achieve permanent academic positions within a few years of graduating
industry_realities.actual_reality: Over 50% plan academic careers but only 6% expect to become assistant professors immediately after PhD, and 46% anticipate a postdoc first — and the actual rate of permanent academic placement has been declining for decades
industry_realities.implication: Every PhD student should build non-academic career options in parallel, regardless of academic career intent — the structural mismatch between aspiration and outcomes is too large to ignore

industry_realities.common_belief: If my target program says their graduates are all employed, the career outcomes are strong
industry_realities.actual_reality: 'Eventually employed' and 'had definite plans at graduation' are dramatically different metrics; humanities (65.8%) and biomedical (68.2%) definite commitment rates mean more than 1 in 3 graduates have no committed plans on graduation day, even if most eventually find something
industry_realities.implication: Request definite commitment rates at graduation — not eventual employment statistics — when evaluating program outcomes; the gap between the two metrics reveals the real level of uncertainty graduates face at the moment it matters most

industry_realities.common_belief: Underrepresented students who leave PhD programs do so because graduate school wasn't right for them
industry_realities.actual_reality: Underrepresented students leave STEMM at higher rates than peers partly due to lack of effective mentorship and identity conflicts with academic culture; this is a structural gap, not an individual capability or fit issue
industry_realities.implication: Underrepresented students should specifically assess whether a program and advisor have demonstrated track records of supporting students with similar backgrounds, and treat the absence of this as a structural risk factor

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD programs provide adequate career guidance for both academic and non-academic paths
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 29% of PhD students received useful non-academic career advice from their program, and 60% relied on personal research for career planning — programs systematically under-deliver on career preparation
industry_realities.implication: Career preparation must be treated as an individual responsibility requiring active external networking, not something the program will provide — students should seek industry contacts and informational interviews independently from day one

industry_realities.common_belief: If academia doesn't work out, a PhD in any field can transition to industry without significant friction
industry_realities.actual_reality: CS/Engineering PhD to industry is near-seamless; biology PhD to industry often requires retraining or skills reframing; humanities PhD to non-academic careers involves a cultural and identity shift that programs actively discourage rather than support
industry_realities.implication: Field selection is a decision about career optionality, not just intellectual interest; the friction cost of non-academic transition must be modeled as part of the PhD decision, not assumed away

industry_realities.common_belief: Your primary advisor is sufficient mentorship for a PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: National Academies research shows that single-mentor models create a single point of failure; PhD students with multiple mentoring relationships — co-advisors, engaged committee members, peer mentors, external professionals — have better outcomes
industry_realities.implication: Students should proactively build multiple mentoring relationships rather than waiting for programs to structure this; and should evaluate programs partly on whether they facilitate or discourage multi-mentor structures

industry_realities.common_belief: Most institutions formally evaluate and hold accountable advisors for mentorship quality
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most institutions do not formally evaluate advisor mentorship quality; widespread adoption of effective mentorship requires systemic shifts that have not occurred in most programs
industry_realities.implication: Students cannot rely on institutional quality control to protect them from poor advisors; self-directed investigation before joining a lab is the primary protection mechanism available

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PhD applications work like US applications — submit to the program, a committee reviews, and an advisor is assigned later
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PhD admissions are supervisor-first: you identify and secure a willing supervisor before applying formally, and the formal application is frequently a paper process ratifying a decision already made. Many programs won't consider applications without a named supervisor.
industry_realities.implication: Applicants must begin supervisor outreach 6–12 months before the formal application deadline, not after submission

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada's 2024 federal budget raised PhD stipends to $40,000/year, making Canadian programs newly competitive with US programs
industry_realities.actual_reality: The $40,000/year increase applies only to Tri-Council award holders (CGRS-D, Vanier). The vast majority of PhD students funded through supervisor research grants see no increase and continue receiving $22,000-$30,000 CAD/year at most institutions
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students must ask specifically whether their funding comes from Tri-Council awards or supervisor grants before treating the $40,000 figure as relevant to their situation

industry_realities.common_belief: A US PhD from a top-ranked program is always the superior choice for international students who want to build a career in North America
industry_realities.actual_reality: For Indian and Chinese nationals, a US PhD often leads to permanent temporary status — cycling through OPT, H-1B lotteries, and EB green card queues that stretch 50+ years — while a Canadian PhD of equivalent research quality leads to PR in 18-30 months
industry_realities.implication: Research program prestige should be evaluated in the context of actual immigration outcomes for your specific country of birth, not in the abstract

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD universally improves your competitiveness in tech hiring
industry_realities.actual_reality: The PhD premium is real and substantial only for research scientist and applied scientist roles; for SWE, data engineering, most PM tracks, and management tracks, the premium is marginal or negative
industry_realities.implication: Students should identify their specific target role before pursuing a PhD — not assume it improves all career options

industry_realities.common_belief: The success stories from a brilliant jerk's lab represent the realistic outcome for a strong, committed student
industry_realities.actual_reality: The success stories are a survivorship-selected sample; the students who left, were harmed, or did not finish are systematically less visible and less connected to the networks prospective students use for advice
industry_realities.implication: The true base rate for positive outcomes must be calculated against all students who entered the lab, not the visible alumni — which requires actively seeking out people who left

industry_realities.common_belief: Co-advising reduces risk by giving the student two mentors instead of one
industry_realities.actual_reality: Co-advising can multiply risk if the advisors have unresolved tensions, conflicting agendas, or split funding — the student absorbs the coordination cost and carries double exposure to single-advisor failure modes
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate co-advising as a structure to be stress-tested, not a safety feature to be assumed — the benefit only materializes under specific conditions that must be verified before committing

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD admissions work like undergraduate admissions — a centralized committee reviews all applications and selects the best candidates based on GPA, test scores, and essays
industry_realities.actual_reality: In most STEM PhD programs, faculty interest is the primary gate for admission. Professors advocate for students they want to fund and work with. A cold application with no prior faculty contact is structurally disadvantaged relative to an application where an advisor already knows the student's name and research interests.
industry_realities.implication: Students should contact potential advisors before submitting applications and confirm interest from at least one faculty member at each program on their list before finalizing where to apply

industry_realities.common_belief: An MS degree always strengthens a PhD application by demonstrating advanced academic capability
industry_realities.actual_reality: In US CS and STEM R1 programs, an MS without a clear research narrative can signal failed direct PhD admission rather than additional qualification; top programs prefer strong direct-entry bachelor's applicants
industry_realities.implication: International students pursuing an MS to improve US PhD competitiveness must produce thesis research output and construct an explicit narrative explaining why the MS was the right path — not just assume the credential speaks for itself

industry_realities.common_belief: An MS degree, regardless of track, strengthens a PhD application
industry_realities.actual_reality: PhD programs evaluate research potential through research evidence — publications, RA experience, thesis work. A coursework-only MS produces none of these. The degree label is not the signal; the research output is.
industry_realities.implication: Students must actively generate research output during any MS program intended as PhD preparation, regardless of whether the program requires it

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD offer letters are fixed — you either accept or decline
industry_realities.actual_reality: Stipend, summer funding, conference travel budget, start date, and coursework waivers are all frequently negotiated by strong candidates, and departments expect it
industry_realities.implication: Every applicant should treat the offer as a starting point and request a follow-up conversation before accepting, not as a binary take-it-or-leave-it decision

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD admissions are globally competitive — the best candidates get in and the rest don't
industry_realities.actual_reality: PhD admissions are locally competitive — admission depends on whether a faculty member in your specific subfield has bandwidth that year; a perfect candidate with no faculty match gets rejected while a moderately competitive candidate with strong faculty alignment gets admitted
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should invest more time identifying and contacting specific faculty than optimizing credentials, because the matching mechanism is person-to-person, not application-to-program

industry_realities.common_belief: Mental health struggles during a PhD are caused by individual weakness, impostor syndrome, or poor personal coping — they are the exception, not the rule
industry_realities.actual_reality: Mental health distress is a structural feature of PhD training, not an individual failure: 36% of PhD students seek help for anxiety or depression related to their PhD, and PhD students are 2.43x more likely to experience depression and anxiety than similarly-educated comparison groups
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should treat mental health risk as a program selection variable to be actively assessed — not as a personal contingency to manage after enrollment

industry_realities.common_belief: Advisor research fit is the most important factor in choosing a PhD program
industry_realities.actual_reality: Research fit is irrelevant if the advisor leaves the institution mid-program; structural factors like tenure status, funded grants, and department support policies determine whether you can actually complete a degree under that advisor
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate structural stability before going deep on research alignment — a structurally unstable situation with perfect research fit is worse than a structurally stable situation with good-but-not-perfect fit

industry_realities.common_belief: Program rankings are a reliable proxy for career outcomes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Rankings measure research output and prestige metrics that predict academic job market success but not industry careers; within PhD programs, advisor relationship and research quality are more predictive than overall rank
industry_realities.implication: Students should research advisor placement records and alumni industry outcomes directly rather than defaulting to rankings as a shortcut

industry_realities.common_belief: A gap year automatically improves your PhD application
industry_realities.actual_reality: A gap year only improves outcomes if it produces measurable new inputs — research experience, a publication or poster, or a meaningful faculty relationship; elapsed time alone does not strengthen an application
industry_realities.implication: Before committing to a gap year, identify precisely what credential or relationship you will produce and verify it is achievable in your specific situation

industry_realities.common_belief: UK PhD funding listed in advertisements is generally available to international students
industry_realities.actual_reality: The majority of UK PhD funding — particularly UKRI studentships — is restricted to UK and EU nationals; 'funding available' in an advertisement almost always means UK/EU only unless explicitly stated otherwise
industry_realities.implication: International students must verify eligibility before preparing any application materials; assume ineligible unless explicitly confirmed otherwise

industry_realities.common_belief: A master's degree always increases lifetime earnings over not having one
industry_realities.actual_reality: 43% of master's degree programs have negative lifetime ROI, and the median bachelor's degree has higher lifetime ROI (~$160K) than most master's degrees, because it costs less and takes less time
industry_realities.implication: Field selection for an MS is not a preference question — it is a financial risk decision; students in negative-ROI fields are paying for a credential that statistically makes them worse off financially

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD funding advice works the same across disciplines — evaluate the advisor's grants and lab first
industry_realities.actual_reality: In humanities, funding flows from departmental cohort packages, not advisor grants — the advisor has little or no discretion over your funding, making the STEM advisor-first logic structurally wrong
industry_realities.implication: Humanities applicants should interrogate department-level funding guarantees, teaching obligation structures, and completion fellowship availability rather than asking about advisor grants

industry_realities.common_belief: Admission to a Canadian PhD program means you are funded
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PhD funding is assembled from multiple sources — supervisor RA grants, TAships, university fellowships, and competitive external awards — and the offer letter may not include a specific funding commitment. Students have arrived without confirmed packages.
industry_realities.implication: Never accept a Canadian PhD offer without a written, specific funding commitment detailing source, amount, and duration

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PhD stipends are lower than US stipends, making Canada a financially inferior option
industry_realities.actual_reality: After adjusting for CAD/USD exchange rate and adding back $2,000-$6,000 in health insurance savings, a $30,000 CAD Canadian stipend is roughly equivalent in real purchasing power to a $22,000-$24,000 USD US stipend with employer-covered insurance
industry_realities.implication: The financial comparison is closer than nominal dollar figures suggest, but still favors US programs at the top end; students should do the adjusted math rather than accepting surface-level comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: The PGWP duration depends on how long your PhD program took
industry_realities.actual_reality: As of February 15, 2024, all master's and PhD graduates from eligible DLIs receive a 3-year PGWP regardless of program length — a 2-year PhD and a 5-year PhD both get exactly 3 years
industry_realities.implication: Students should not time their graduation or program completion to maximize PGWP duration under the old rules — the new flat 3-year policy removes that calculation

industry_realities.common_belief: Program ranking is the dominant variable in PhD outcome quality
industry_realities.actual_reality: For industry research track, a rank-30 program with an advisor who actively places students at Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta AI can outperform a rank-10 program whose advisor has no industry relationships
industry_realities.implication: Industry-track students should weight advisor-specific placement history and industry connections more heavily than aggregate program rank

industry_realities.common_belief: A prominent advisor's placement network advantage is durable and will benefit any student who completes a PhD under them
industry_realities.actual_reality: The placement advantage is partially dependent on the advisor writing strong advocacy letters; students with strained relationships often receive lukewarm letters that neutralize the prestige benefit, and for non-academic careers the name effect decays within 2–3 years
industry_realities.implication: The prestige premium must be stress-tested against the likelihood of a strained relationship and the specific career path being targeted before it can be counted as a reliable benefit

industry_realities.common_belief: Having two advisors means twice as much mentorship and guidance
industry_realities.actual_reality: Diffuse accountability means each advisor assumes the other is handling critical issues — response times slow, meetings get cancelled, and annual reviews surface gaps that neither advisor owned
industry_realities.implication: Establish a formal primary advisor of record and require joint meetings on a regular cadence; do not manage two separate relationships and expect the sum to equal comprehensive mentorship

industry_realities.common_belief: A world-class program (high ranking) produces better outcomes than a lower-ranked program regardless of other factors
industry_realities.actual_reality: A world-class program with a bad advisor produces a worse outcome than a good program with an exceptional advisor. The advisor relationship is the primary determinant of PhD outcomes — not program prestige.
industry_realities.implication: Students should weight advisor quality, mentorship track record, and placement outcomes above program ranking when making PhD program decisions

industry_realities.common_belief: A master's degree is a reliable financial investment that increases lifetime earnings
industry_realities.actual_reality: 43% of master's programs yield negative financial returns when total cost including opportunity cost is calculated; ROI is highly field-dependent and frequently negative in humanities, education, and arts
industry_realities.implication: ROI analysis must be done field-specifically and must include foregone salary as a cost component, not just tuition; the decision to pursue an MS should not be made on the assumption that it generically pays off

industry_realities.common_belief: A 'master's by project' is equivalent to a thesis MS for PhD applications
industry_realities.actual_reality: PhD programs treat project-track and thesis-track MS degrees inconsistently — some accept project work as research evidence, many do not. There is no standard.
industry_realities.implication: Students must verify with each target PhD program individually before relying on project-track work as PhD application evidence

industry_realities.common_belief: The program with the highest stated stipend has the best financial offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: A 9-month stipend can be worth thousands less annually than a lower 12-month stipend when annualized, before accounting for conference travel support and summer funding availability
industry_realities.implication: Always convert all offers to true annualized value including summer coverage before making financial comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: The most prestigious advisor at the best-ranked program produces the best PhD outcome
industry_realities.actual_reality: Faculty are hired for research and grant-funding ability, not advising quality; some of the most cited professors at top-ranked programs are the worst mentors; a mediocre program with an excellent mentor produces better PhD outcomes than a top-ranked program with a negligent or toxic advisor
industry_realities.implication: Advising quality must be evaluated independently of ranking and citation metrics using placement records, publication authorship patterns, and direct student testimony

industry_realities.common_belief: The advisor relationship is one of several factors affecting PhD quality, roughly comparable in importance to program ranking, research fit, and funding
industry_realities.actual_reality: The advisor relationship is the single strongest predictor of PhD student mental health outcomes — stronger than funding, program rank, or research area; 43% of students with negative or unsupportive advisors met criteria for moderate-severe anxiety
industry_realities.implication: Advisor assessment deserves disproportionate weight in program selection decisions relative to the attention most applicants give it

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking a prospective advisor about their tenure status is rude or inappropriate
industry_realities.actual_reality: It is a professional question with direct relevance to your decision; any advisor with a healthy relationship with students will answer directly, and evasiveness is itself informative
industry_realities.implication: Ask directly and early; frame it as due diligence, not distrust — the response reveals both the factual answer and something about how the advisor handles uncomfortable professional conversations

industry_realities.common_belief: A Masters degree from a top-brand university is a safe investment that will pay off
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many professional MS programs are revenue-generating tuition programs with no funding; total cost can exceed $200,000 for international students; employment outcomes are not guaranteed and OPT deadlines create time pressure
industry_realities.implication: International students must calculate actual ROI using real placement data and compare against the funded PhD alternative before committing

industry_realities.common_belief: Prestige of program is the primary determinant of PhD career outcomes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Advisor match, funding security, and research fit are more predictive of outcomes for most career paths than program ranking — a funded PhD with a strong advisor at rank 20 typically outperforms an unfunded or advisor-mismatched one at rank 5
industry_realities.implication: Do not decline a funded, well-matched offer for a prestigious but worse-fit or unfunded alternative without verifying that your specific target role requires the higher-ranked institution

industry_realities.common_belief: A shorter PhD (3–4 years in UK/EU) means less work and lower pressure
industry_realities.actual_reality: Shorter PhDs require research productivity almost immediately — there is no coursework buffer or rotation period; the compressed timeline means the first year must produce usable results, creating higher immediate pressure than a US program's first year
industry_realities.implication: Only students with well-developed research questions, strong prior experimental or methodological skills, and high self-direction should pursue UK/EU PhDs; students who need structured learning time are likely to struggle

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting a job in the US after graduation is primarily a skills and networking problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: International students apply to 2x as many jobs but receive 30% fewer offers than domestic students, and the primary cause is sponsorship requirement, not skill gap — this is a structural constraint, not a performance gap
industry_realities.implication: Improving your resume or networking harder does not solve the sponsorship problem; job search strategy must be built around targeting only known H-1B sponsors from the start

industry_realities.common_belief: A 5-year funded humanities PhD offer means you can complete the degree in 5 years with funding
industry_realities.actual_reality: Median humanities time-to-degree is 8.4–9.5 years; a 5-year funding package covers roughly 55% of the typical completion timeline — years 6–9 require competitive external fellowships, adjuncting, or personal savings
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should explicitly ask what happens in years 6–8, what percentage of recent cohorts finished within the funding window, and what the department's dissertation completion fellowship looks like before accepting any offer

industry_realities.common_belief: The application deadline is the key date to track for a Canadian PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: Internal funding competitions (OGS, institutional scholarships) close in October–November, months before program application deadlines of December–January. Missing the funding deadline is not recoverable within that cycle.
industry_realities.implication: The funding calendar must be obtained from the department graduate coordinator before October, making it the first administrative action after identifying target schools

industry_realities.common_belief: The stipend listed in a PhD offer letter is what you will receive throughout your program
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PhD offers frequently include competitive fellowship amounts that are not guaranteed; the baseline institutional guarantee is often $5,000-$15,000 CAD/year less than the headline figure
industry_realities.implication: Students must explicitly ask for the guaranteed funding floor and assess livability on that basis, not the advertised package

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PR through Express Entry requires a job offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: CEC requires only 1 year of skilled Canadian work experience — no job offer is required to receive an ITA or to apply for PR; a job offer adds 25-50 CRS points but is not mandatory
industry_realities.implication: PhD graduates should not wait to secure a formal job offer before creating an Express Entry profile; eligible profiles can receive ITAs without one

industry_realities.common_belief: The academic faculty path takes 5–7 years and then you get a faculty job
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most CS faculty positions require a postdoc (1–3 years at $55K–$80K) after the PhD — total timeline to first faculty salary is often 8–10 years
industry_realities.implication: Students planning for academic careers should model the full timeline including postdoc years when evaluating the financial and career trajectory

industry_realities.common_belief: Institutional support structures — formal co-advisors, DGS oversight, departmental grievance processes — provide a reliable safety net against advisor toxicity
industry_realities.actual_reality: DGS deference to powerful faculty is common; formal mechanisms that exist on paper are frequently unavailable in practice when a high-profile or grant-productive advisor is involved
industry_realities.implication: Support structure viability must be verified through actual examples of past intervention, not the existence of formal roles

industry_realities.common_belief: Faculty who agree to co-advise have already worked out how to do it
industry_realities.actual_reality: Co-advising is often proposed by one faculty member without prior discussion with the other, or agreed to without resolving disagreements about research direction, milestone standards, or role division
industry_realities.implication: Ask directly whether the two proposed co-advisors have discussed the specific arrangement for your project together — the answer is often no

industry_realities.common_belief: A fellowship offer means your funding is secure for the duration of your PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: University fellowships are typically 1-year awards given to top incoming students — not multi-year guarantees. After year one, students typically transition to RA or TA funding under conditions that may not have been clearly specified at the time of the offer.
industry_realities.implication: Students must ask explicitly about multi-year funding continuity and understand what mechanism will replace fellowship funding after year one

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD is required for senior roles at top tech companies in ML and AI
industry_realities.actual_reality: Industry data scientist, ML engineer, and software engineer roles at top tech companies rarely require a PhD; a terminal MS is sufficient for most non-research-track positions
industry_realities.implication: Applicants targeting industry AI/ML careers should evaluate whether the additional cost and time of a PhD (and the stepping-stone MS leading to it) is justified by the specific roles they want, rather than assuming PhD is the default credential for technical seniority

industry_realities.common_belief: Coursework MS and thesis MS are two names for the same thing
industry_realities.actual_reality: They are structurally different programs that train different skills, produce different credentials, carry different costs, and lead to different career outcomes. The shared label 'Master's degree' obscures these differences.
industry_realities.implication: Applicants must investigate the specific track structure of any MS program — not just its name — before applying

industry_realities.common_belief: Mentioning a competing offer is aggressive or off-putting in academic culture
industry_realities.actual_reality: Disclosing a specific competing offer is the single most effective negotiation lever and is considered professional by admissions committees and advisors, especially in STEM
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should state competing offers explicitly with specific numbers rather than hinting at alternatives or staying silent out of perceived politeness

industry_realities.common_belief: A recommendation letter from a Nobel laureate or highly famous researcher carries maximum weight
industry_realities.actual_reality: Committees read letters as informal peer reviews; a letter from a prominent researcher who barely knows you is worth less than a letter from a less prominent researcher who supervised your thesis and can speak specifically to your capability
industry_realities.implication: Choose recommenders for supervisory depth and ability to make specific claims about your research capability, not for name recognition

industry_realities.common_belief: Surviving a tough advisor is a rite of passage that builds resilience and is widely validated by successful people in the field
industry_realities.actual_reality: Survival narratives are selection-biased: only the people who survived are available to describe the experience; the people most damaged by toxic advisors left the field and are absent from the professional networks that applicants consult
industry_realities.implication: Positive testimonials about difficult advisors should be discounted for survivorship bias; applicants should specifically seek out information about students who left the lab or program

industry_realities.common_belief: If your advisor leaves, the department will take care of you
industry_realities.actual_reality: Departments vary enormously in their actual support infrastructure; some have clear bridge funding policies, others leave students to navigate the situation ad hoc with the DGS as a starting point but no guaranteed resources
industry_realities.implication: Ask the department for their written policy before accepting an offer, not after a crisis — and treat vague or dismissive answers as a negative signal about the department's track record on this

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD programs at top schools provide funding to all admitted students
industry_realities.actual_reality: Some PhD programs admit students without guaranteed funding, expecting them to find RA or TA positions after enrollment; funding can also disappear if the advisor loses grant support
industry_realities.implication: Students must verify the funding structure explicitly — whether stipend is guaranteed, for how many years, and at what institutional level — before accepting any offer

industry_realities.common_belief: The April 15 deadline is a bureaucratic formality
industry_realities.actual_reality: The CGS April 15 Resolution is an ethical commitment — declining before that date allows waitlisted candidates to receive offers in time; late declines have real consequences for other applicants and for your professional reputation in the field
industry_realities.implication: Make your decision and communicate it before April 15, regardless of how uncomfortable the conversation feels

industry_realities.common_belief: European PhD salary/employment structures are similar to US PhD stipends
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many EU PhD positions — particularly in Germany, Netherlands, and Sweden — are formal employment contracts with social security contributions, healthcare benefits, and legal worker protections; these are structurally different from US stipends and have long-term immigration and benefits implications
industry_realities.implication: Students should explicitly ask whether a position is an Arbeitsvertrag/employment contract rather than a scholarship, because the financial security, social insurance accumulation, and visa implications differ significantly

industry_realities.common_belief: STEM OPT gives you 3 H-1B attempts, so most people eventually get selected
industry_realities.actual_reality: At entry-level selection rates of ~15%, cumulative probability of at least one selection in 3 attempts is ~39%, meaning approximately 6 in 10 entry-level international graduates with STEM OPT will exhaust all attempts without an H-1B
industry_realities.implication: Plan B is not a pessimistic contingency — it is the statistically more likely outcome for entry-level international graduates and should be planned with equal seriousness to Plan A

industry_realities.common_belief: Strong individual research can overcome program rank in the academic job market
industry_realities.actual_reality: Humanities hiring committees routinely filter applications by institutional affiliation at early screening stages — unlike STEM, where strong publications can partially offset program rank, humanities program prestige shapes whether applications are reviewed at all
industry_realities.implication: Applicants targeting tenure-track academic careers in humanities should weight program rank more heavily than is common advice in domain-general PhD application guides

industry_realities.common_belief: GRE scores are a standard part of PhD applications internationally
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most Canadian PhD programs do not require the GRE. It is not a standard requirement in the Canadian system.
industry_realities.implication: Applicants targeting Canadian programs should verify requirements before investing in GRE preparation, and should reallocate that time to supervisor outreach and research materials

industry_realities.common_belief: Major Canadian research universities (UofT, UBC) offer the best financial conditions for PhD students because they have the largest budgets
industry_realities.actual_reality: UofT and UBC are located in Canada's two most expensive cities; their higher nominal stipends are substantially offset by rent that can consume 80-100% of monthly take-home pay. McGill (Montreal) and University of Waterloo often provide better real purchasing power despite lower headline numbers
industry_realities.implication: Ranking programs by nominal stipend without adjusting for city cost of living produces systematically misleading financial comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD and a master's degree are treated the same way in Canada's immigration points system
industry_realities.actual_reality: A PhD earns 150 CRS points vs. 135 for a master's — a 15-point differential that is meaningful in competitive Express Entry draws where cutoffs shift by single digits
industry_realities.implication: The PhD credential itself provides a concrete, quantified immigration advantage in Canada beyond its research and career value

industry_realities.common_belief: If a PhD advisor says their students 'go to industry,' that means they have strong industry research placement
industry_realities.actual_reality: Industry placements range from SWE/product roles to top AI lab research scientist positions — these are vastly different outcomes that advisors routinely conflate in their claims
industry_realities.implication: Always ask specifically about research scientist placements at named top labs, not just general 'industry' placements; verify on LinkedIn

industry_realities.common_belief: 'It was hard but it made me stronger' testimonials from successful alumni are reliable evidence that a difficult advisor is survivable
industry_realities.actual_reality: These testimonials reflect survivorship selection and cognitive dissonance reduction; they systematically underrepresent the harm experienced by students who did not survive, and the 'growth through adversity' framing is a post-hoc rationalization common among people who endured significant cost
industry_realities.implication: Weight these testimonials as evidence of what is possible for some students, not as evidence of what is probable for you

industry_realities.common_belief: Advisor conflicts are rare and can be managed if they arise
industry_realities.actual_reality: If two advisors have unspoken professional tensions, the student becomes the default communication channel — not because anyone decides this, but because it is structurally easier for each advisor than addressing the conflict directly
industry_realities.implication: Investigate the interpersonal dynamic between prospective co-advisors before committing, not just their individual reputations and research fit

industry_realities.common_belief: NSF GRFP is an external fellowship option that international PhD students should pursue
industry_realities.actual_reality: NSF GRFP is restricted to US citizens and permanent residents. International students are ineligible.
industry_realities.implication: International students should research fellowship eligibility explicitly before investing time in applications; do not assume that prestigious fellowships are universally accessible

industry_realities.common_belief: MFA, MSW, MLIS, and MPA are 'lesser' degrees than a PhD in prestige terms
industry_realities.actual_reality: In their respective fields, these are the terminal professional credentials — they are the highest credential required and often more valued than a PhD for practice roles
industry_realities.implication: Applicants in creative, social work, library science, or public administration fields should not treat the absence of a PhD as a credential gap; pursuing a PhD in these fields when a terminal master's is the professional norm is often counterproductive

industry_realities.common_belief: MS funding (TA/RA) is common, similar to PhD funding
industry_realities.actual_reality: Coursework MS programs almost never offer funding; thesis MS programs offer it only occasionally. MS funding is the exception, not the rule, unlike PhD programs where full funding is the norm in many fields.
industry_realities.implication: International students budgeting for an MS should plan for full self-funding unless they have explicitly confirmed funding availability for their specific program and track

industry_realities.common_belief: Visit weekends are primarily social events to help you get a feel for the program culture
industry_realities.actual_reality: The visit is your only real due diligence window before a 5+ year commitment; it is an evaluation opportunity that most applicants underuse by avoiding critical questions
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should prepare specific diagnostic questions for advanced PhD students — about advisor responsiveness, funding gaps, graduation timelines — and treat the visit as structured investigation, not celebration

industry_realities.common_belief: Initial application review is a thorough holistic evaluation of each file
industry_realities.actual_reality: Initial screening takes 30–60 seconds per file; reviewers scan for GPA trends, research clarity, writing quality, and completion likelihood before most applications receive deeper evaluation
industry_realities.implication: The SOP opening, clear research direction, and application presentation must be immediately legible — applicants cannot rely on reviewers discovering strengths buried in a lengthy narrative

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD program with high output, prestigious publications, and strong placement statistics is a well-functioning program with good advising
industry_realities.actual_reality: High lab output and strong placement statistics can coexist with Exploiter advising patterns; aggregate program prestige metrics do not differentiate between advisors who develop students and advisors who extract student labor while producing strong lab-level outcomes
industry_realities.implication: Program-level metrics must be disaggregated to the advisor level to be useful for predicting individual student experience

industry_realities.common_belief: Pre-tenure advisors are riskier choices and should generally be avoided
industry_realities.actual_reality: Pre-tenure advisors offer genuine benefits — higher personal investment, greater accessibility, near-peer collaboration, faster-moving research — and can be excellent choices when risk is assessed and mitigated proactively
industry_realities.implication: The decision is not binary avoid/accept; it is about accurately pricing the risk, verifying the mitigating factors (prior graduates, active grants, years on clock), and building proactive infrastructure if you proceed

industry_realities.common_belief: Prestige transfers universally across career contexts
industry_realities.actual_reality: Rankings matter specifically for academic hiring pipelines, elite consulting/finance recruiting, and home-country brand recognition — they are largely irrelevant for most US industry employers who screen on skills and projects
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should map the specific career context they're targeting and determine whether rank is an actual screening filter in that context before weighting it heavily

industry_realities.common_belief: Fixing your GRE score is a high-ROI improvement for reapplication
industry_realities.actual_reality: GRE importance is declining at most programs and a score improvement alone rarely changes admission outcomes at competitive programs; research experience and faculty relationships carry far more weight
industry_realities.implication: Do not plan a gap year around GRE improvement as the primary strategy — treat it as a supplement to substantive research credential building, not a substitute

industry_realities.common_belief: Completing a PhD at a prestigious European institution gives equivalent academic job market positioning as a US PhD for US academic positions
industry_realities.actual_reality: US PhD programs have structural advantages for US academic placements through advisor network effects, letter-writer recognition, and conference ecosystem presence; European PhD holders face measurable friction when competing for US academic jobs against US-trained graduates
industry_realities.implication: Students who want to pursue US academic careers should weight US PhD programs more heavily unless they have exceptional European advisors with strong US networks, or are targeting fields where European training is particularly prestigious

industry_realities.common_belief: Any program called 'Data Science,' 'Analytics,' or 'Applied Computing' qualifies for STEM OPT
industry_realities.actual_reality: STEM OPT eligibility is determined by the program's CIP code, not its name or marketing; a Data Analytics MS in a business school may have a non-STEM CIP code and not qualify
industry_realities.implication: Never assume STEM OPT eligibility from the program name — verify the CIP code with the DSO before enrolling, as this decision cannot be easily corrected after the fact

industry_realities.common_belief: A prestigious advisor ensures strong job market outcomes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Advisor job placement record (specific students placed into tenure-track positions) and subfield alignment are distinct from personal prestige — an advisor can be prominent while having placed no students recently or while working in a tangential subfield
industry_realities.implication: Ask directly how many students the prospective advisor has placed into tenure-track positions in the past 5 years, and verify that their recent work actually engages your project's scholarly concerns

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking a prospective supervisor about their funding status is presumptuous or rude
industry_realities.actual_reality: In the Canadian PhD context, where funding flows directly from the supervisor's grant, asking about RA funding availability is considered responsible due diligence, not impolite. The financial dimension of the supervisor relationship is more explicit in Canada than in the US.
industry_realities.implication: Directly ask prospective supervisors 'Do you have RA funding available for incoming students?' during the initial call — this is expected and appropriate

industry_realities.common_belief: TAship income is free money added to research stipend that improves PhD financial conditions
industry_realities.actual_reality: TAships are labor that consumes 10-20 hours per week during term; students who rely on TA income to meet basic expenses are effectively trading research time for survival income, which extends time-to-degree and increases total cost of the PhD
industry_realities.implication: TAship dependency should be treated as a financial red flag about the base stipend level, not a feature of the offer

industry_realities.common_belief: Any work experience in Canada while on PGWP counts toward Express Entry eligibility
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only work in NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupations counts toward the CEC 1,560-hour requirement; TEER 4 and 5 roles (which include many service and administrative jobs) are entirely excluded
industry_realities.implication: PhD graduates must verify their occupation's NOC TEER category before accepting employment, especially if considering interim work while searching for a role in their field

industry_realities.common_belief: The standard PhD application process is the only path into industry research labs
industry_realities.actual_reality: Since ~2020, major AI labs have established formal co-supervision programs, residency programs, and PhD fellowships — these are structurally distinct tracks with supplemented compensation and applied research
industry_realities.implication: Students targeting specific industry labs should research and apply to these programs directly before defaulting to standard university PhD applications

industry_realities.common_belief: The PhD admissions decision is reversible enough that you can try a difficult advisor and switch if it doesn't work out
industry_realities.actual_reality: The window for easy advisor switching closes progressively after year 1–2; by the time many students recognize the full extent of the harm, they have accumulated sunk costs — completed coursework, preliminary exams, research commitments — that make switching or leaving psychologically and practically very costly
industry_realities.implication: The decision should be made as if it is more irreversible than it formally appears, because the psychological barriers to exit increase substantially after the relationship is established

industry_realities.common_belief: Dissertation milestone standards are consistent across a program
industry_realities.actual_reality: Co-advisors from different departments may apply their own department's norms to qualifying exams, proposals, and defenses — creating ambiguity that surfaces at the highest-stakes moments
industry_realities.implication: Negotiate and document milestone standards in writing with both advisors before advancing, not at the point when ambiguity becomes a problem

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD is always more prestigious and career-valuable than a Masters, so when in doubt, pursue the PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: For students targeting industry employment within 2 years with a specific technical skill need, a well-placed MS program may provide faster, lower-risk career entry than a 5–6 year PhD with 40–50% dropout rates. The PhD is not superior in all career contexts.
industry_realities.implication: Students should map their target job titles and timelines first, then determine which credential structure — MS or PhD — is actually required or preferred by employers in that specific sector

industry_realities.common_belief: Doing an MS after PhD rejection and then reapplying is a reliable strategy for eventual PhD admission
industry_realities.actual_reality: It works only if the MS is thesis-based, produces new research evidence, and the applicant honestly addresses the specific weakness that caused the original rejection; a coursework MS does not fix weak undergraduate research and produces the same application profile
industry_realities.implication: Applicants considering this path must first honestly diagnose what caused the rejection, then verify that the specific MS program will generate the type of evidence needed to address it

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher salary outcome from an MS degree means the financial investment is straightforwardly worth it
industry_realities.actual_reality: The net return depends on total cost (tuition + living + opportunity cost) relative to the salary premium over what you would earn without the degree. For international students paying $30,000–$80,000 in tuition alone, the break-even timeline is longer than headline salary figures suggest.
industry_realities.implication: Students should calculate break-even timelines — not just compare salary figures — when evaluating whether the MS investment is financially justified

industry_realities.common_belief: Union-negotiated TA stipends can be supplemented or improved through negotiation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Stipends fixed by collective bargaining agreements are legally binding and cannot be changed by individual department or advisor discretion, regardless of competing offers
industry_realities.implication: When funding is TA-based in a unionized program, redirect negotiation entirely to non-stipend dimensions rather than wasting leverage on an immovable number

industry_realities.common_belief: A high GPA is the most important academic signal in PhD admissions
industry_realities.actual_reality: GPA trends matter more than GPA peaks — reviewers look for improvement as a signal of intellectual maturity and completion likelihood; a rising trajectory often outweighs a higher but flat or declining one
industry_realities.implication: Applicants with early academic struggles but strong recent performance should explicitly frame their trajectory in the SOP rather than hoping reviewers will notice the pattern independently

industry_realities.common_belief: University counseling services are available and accessible to PhD students who need support
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most universities have general CAPS services that share capacity with the undergraduate population, creating long wait times and limited graduate-student-specific expertise; dedicated PhD counseling slots are an indicator of institutional seriousness about the problem, not a universal baseline
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should explicitly verify whether graduate-specific counseling slots exist — not just whether a university has a counseling center

industry_realities.common_belief: For international students, advisor departure is primarily an academic problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: Advisor departure triggers simultaneous academic, financial, and immigration complications; I-20 transfer, SEVIS re-registration, and OPT timeline disruption are all activated by the same event that domestic students experience as purely academic
industry_realities.implication: International students must explicitly raise visa implications with their prospective advisor before accepting an offer — this dimension will not be raised for them, and the cost of not knowing is higher than for domestic students

industry_realities.common_belief: A well-known advisor with many students is a better mentor
industry_realities.actual_reality: Highly productive advisors with large labs often cannot give adequate individual mentorship — advising quality per student decreases as lab size increases
industry_realities.implication: Students should assess advisor-to-student ratio and meeting frequency directly, not infer mentorship quality from advisor prestige or publication count

industry_realities.common_belief: The 'accept and transfer' strategy is uncommon or unacceptable
industry_realities.actual_reality: Accepting a funded offer, generating research output in year 1, and reapplying to target programs is a legitimate and often more efficient path than a cold gap year — it maintains income, produces real research credentials, and avoids total loss if the transfer doesn't succeed
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate the accept-and-transfer path before defaulting to declining; the risks are manageable with honest advisor communication upfront

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada is just a lower-stipend version of a US PhD with fewer opportunities
industry_realities.actual_reality: For international students from high-backlog nationalities, Canada's combination of PGWP + Express Entry creates a PR pathway that can be completed in 3–5 years post-PhD, compared to potentially 20–40-year waits under US EB categories — this is a structural difference, not a marginal one
industry_realities.implication: Students from India and China should treat Canadian PhD programs as a primary option rather than a fallback, and explicitly compare immigration timelines rather than treating the US as the default aspirational choice

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting H-1B sponsorship from any employer counts the same
industry_realities.actual_reality: Small and mid-size companies often cannot or will not sponsor H-1B due to cost ($2,200–$6,400+ per petition plus attorney fees) and administrative burden; targeting them on OPT leads to a dead end when H-1B is required
industry_realities.implication: For international students, employer size and H-1B sponsorship history must be treated as primary hiring filters, not secondary considerations after role fit and compensation

industry_realities.common_belief: Tenure-track academic placement is a realistic outcome from a humanities PhD at a good program
industry_realities.actual_reality: English PhD programs produce approximately 1,000 PhDs per year against 200–400 tenure-track openings — placement rates at even top programs are 30–50%; this is a structural supply/demand imbalance, not a temporary market condition
industry_realities.implication: Every humanities PhD applicant should explicitly model non-academic career paths before committing to the degree, and assess whether those paths are acceptable outcomes given a 9-year time investment

industry_realities.common_belief: All major Canadian research universities offer equivalent immigration advantages for international PhD students
industry_realities.actual_reality: Institution location materially affects post-graduation immigration strategy — some Provincial Nominee Programs favor graduates from outside Toronto and Vancouver, meaning a smaller institution in a different province may offer a faster or more accessible PR pathway for certain immigration goals.
industry_realities.implication: Institution location should be evaluated as an immigration strategy variable, not just a prestige or research quality variable, for international students planning to stay in Canada

industry_realities.common_belief: 90% of PhD students at major Canadian universities receive full funding covering tuition and living expenses
industry_realities.actual_reality: A 2023 national survey found nearly 90% of Canadian graduate students reported financial stress, with almost one-third considering leaving academia due to money pressures — indicating that nominal funding coverage does not translate to actual financial adequacy
industry_realities.implication: Coverage of tuition and provision of a stipend does not mean the stipend is livable; students must assess the actual dollar amounts against real cost of living, not just whether funding exists

industry_realities.common_belief: Express Entry is the only federal pathway to PR for PhD graduates in Canada
industry_realities.actual_reality: 11 of 13 provinces operate PNP streams, some specifically designed for PhD graduates with no job offer requirement; a PNP nomination adds 600 CRS points and effectively guarantees selection in any Express Entry draw
industry_realities.implication: PhD graduates should evaluate PNP eligibility in parallel with Express Entry — particularly Ontario and BC streams available directly at graduation — rather than treating CEC as the default single pathway

industry_realities.common_belief: Teaching assistant experience is universally valuable in a PhD program
industry_realities.actual_reality: TA experience is an asset on the academic track and a neutral-to-irrelevant factor on the industry research track — the time cost of TAing is a real tradeoff against research output
industry_realities.implication: Industry-track students should assess whether TA requirements in their program compete with internship time or research output

industry_realities.common_belief: Students who are harmed by difficult advisors would have recognized the warning signs in advance if they had looked carefully enough
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruitment weekends and initial meetings are contexts that actively suppress the signals of toxic behavior; advisors seeking strong students present performative warmth, and the formal setting makes candid observation nearly impossible
industry_realities.implication: Due diligence must go beyond recruitment interactions to include observations of the advisor with current students in unstructured settings, and direct contact with former students who were not referred by the advisor

industry_realities.common_belief: A secondary co-advisor can be added later if needed
industry_realities.actual_reality: A co-advisor recruited during a crisis has no institutional history with the student's work, limited capacity to intervene in an existing advisor dynamic, and enters in a reactive rather than formative role
industry_realities.implication: Identify and recruit a defensive secondary co-advisor before starting the program, not after the primary relationship deteriorates

industry_realities.common_belief: Program location is primarily a lifestyle consideration — the actual degree and credential is what matters for career outcomes
industry_realities.actual_reality: During the OPT window (12–36 months post-graduation), students must find employment within a constrained timeframe. Programs in major tech hubs have structural recruiting advantages — denser employer networks, stronger alumni presence, and on-campus recruiting from target employers — that translate to a 3–6 month practical job search advantage.
industry_realities.implication: For international students dependent on OPT, program location should be treated as a career infrastructure variable, not a lifestyle preference — especially for students without existing US employer networks

industry_realities.common_belief: Conference travel support is a minor perk that doesn't significantly affect the PhD experience
industry_realities.actual_reality: Conference travel support ranging from $500 to $5,000/year creates compounding inequity over 5 years in networking, visibility, and professional opportunity — students who self-fund are systematically disadvantaged
industry_realities.implication: Conference travel support should be explicitly asked about and factored into total offer comparisons as a meaningful compensation variable

industry_realities.common_belief: Applying to more programs always improves your chances
industry_realities.actual_reality: 8–12 programs is the effective range; fewer risks complete rejection in a bad year, but beyond 12 the returns diminish and costs increase without meaningful probability improvement
industry_realities.implication: Portfolio construction should focus on balance (ambitious/solid/safety) and faculty fit per program, not raw application volume

industry_realities.common_belief: If students were experiencing serious problems with an advisor, they would use formal escalation pathways like the DGS or ombudsperson
industry_realities.actual_reality: Emotionally volatile and abusive advisors create hypervigilance and avoidance of bringing problems forward; students often do not escalate because they fear retaliation, do not know the pathways exist, or have internalized the dysfunction as their own failure
industry_realities.implication: The absence of reported problems or formal complaints about an advisor should not be interpreted as evidence that no problems exist

industry_realities.common_belief: A co-advisor relationship can be set up as a contingency if something goes wrong
industry_realities.actual_reality: A relationship formed in crisis after advisor departure is worth substantially less than one built over years of genuine mentorship; faculty who barely know a student cannot advocate effectively, take on advising mid-project meaningfully, or write strong letters
industry_realities.implication: Establish a co-advisor relationship with a tenured faculty member from the start of the program as proactive infrastructure, not as a reactive fallback — the value of the relationship depends on its depth at the moment it is needed

industry_realities.common_belief: Program quality is uniform across the department
industry_realities.actual_reality: PhD experiences are highly advisor-specific — two students in the same top-10 department can have radically different outcomes based on their advisor's grant status, mentorship quality, and professional network
industry_realities.implication: Program-level evaluation is insufficient; students must evaluate the specific advisor relationship as the primary unit of analysis

industry_realities.common_belief: International students can easily take a US-based gap year after their program ends
industry_realities.actual_reality: A gap year for international students has significant visa complications — without remaining OPT, staying in the US may not be legally possible, and re-entry after returning home requires a full visa process
industry_realities.implication: International students must assess visa status as a first-order variable in the gap year decision, not an afterthought

industry_realities.common_belief: The UK Graduate Route visa is a minor benefit of completing a UK PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: The Graduate Route provides 2 years (3 for PhD holders) of open work authorization with no employer e-verify requirement, no lottery, and no cap — it is structurally more accessible than US OPT/STEM OPT and allows genuine open-market job searching
industry_realities.implication: For students considering UK vs. US, the Graduate Route's reliability and openness is a meaningful advantage over OPT/H-1B dependency, particularly for students in fields with lower H-1B sponsorship rates

industry_realities.common_belief: Indian and Chinese nationals who get H-1B sponsorship have solved the immigration problem
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B is a temporary status; EB-2/EB-3 green card backlogs for India and China exceed 50 years at current rates, meaning H-1B holders from these countries cannot realistically achieve permanent residency through employment-based pathways
industry_realities.implication: Indian and Chinese nationals should model their US career as H-1B-capped with no green card endpoint, and evaluate whether that scenario still justifies the investment and life disruption of an unfunded MS

industry_realities.common_belief: Teaching assistantships are a minor component of the PhD experience
industry_realities.actual_reality: Humanities PhD students typically teach 1–2 sections per semester in years 3–5, requiring 10–20 hours per week — this is a substantial work obligation that directly competes with dissertation writing and is the primary mechanism through which time-to-degree extends beyond the funding window
industry_realities.implication: Teaching load is a first-order variable in program evaluation, not a footnote — negotiate which years require teaching and whether any year is protected as a dissertation-only fellowship year

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian and US PhDs take roughly the same time to complete
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PhDs (entered after a master's) typically complete in 4–5 years; US PhDs (entered from bachelor's) take 5–6 years with 2+ years of coursework first. The Canadian system involves lighter required coursework and earlier research engagement from day one.
industry_realities.implication: Applicants choosing between Canadian and US programs should account for the total time-to-degree differential, which affects career entry timing, funding duration requirements, and immigration timeline calculations

industry_realities.common_belief: Quebec universities offering world-class research programs provide the same immigration pathway as universities in Ontario or BC
industry_realities.actual_reality: Quebec operates a completely separate provincial immigration system; federal Express Entry CEC does not apply; French language proficiency is near-mandatory and a distinct CSQ process is required
industry_realities.implication: Students considering Quebec programs must research the CSQ pathway and French language requirements before enrollment, not after graduation

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD compensation eventually catches up with industry SWE compensation
industry_realities.actual_reality: The stipend-to-industry-SWE gap during the PhD represents $500K–$600K in pretax foregone earnings over 4–5 years, and PhD SWEs and MS SWEs are paid identically at the same level at most companies
industry_realities.implication: The financial calculus only favors the PhD for roles where a PhD is a hard requirement (research scientist) or provides a structural premium — not for general engineering roles

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B advanced degree exemption means any Masters degree from a US university improves lottery odds equally
industry_realities.actual_reality: Under post-2025 wage-weighted H-1B lottery systems, PhD graduates entering at higher salary levels (OEWS Level III–IV) have better odds. The type of degree and the salary it commands interact with the lottery mechanics — a PhD at a higher salary tier is meaningfully advantaged over an MS at a lower salary tier.
